articles.title: English councils displaying only one in 20 publicly owned artworks
articles.summary: More than 500,000 pieces of art are owned by 225 councils, the BBC finds, but most of it is storage.
articles.body:
Fewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found.

More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage.

Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK.

Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art.

Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley.

Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council.

Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds.

As of April, just 26,856 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have?

Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display.

All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April.

Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities.

"If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said.

"It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think."

Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset.

"We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people."

The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection.

Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years.

Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24.

The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of.

For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools.

When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection.

Kent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April.

At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept.

"I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so."

The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North.

The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives".

Art UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks .

Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art.

"We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place.

"The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time.

"From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it."

He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances.

Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits.

But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums".

Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26.

Keeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work.

Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display.

One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum .

Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works.

Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public.

That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events.

It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation.

Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme.

"We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on."

Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council.

"A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said.

Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time.

"Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment."

articles.title: Australia vs New Zealand: Age-old rivalry bookends Rugby League World Cup but will it end 18 years of supremacy?
articles.summary: In the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup finals Australia will take on New Zealand; the last time both New Zealand teams won the tournament was back in 2008, nearly two decades ago; the finals take place on Sunday November 16
articles.body:
In a sensational opener to the tournament, Australia clinched a dramatic 24-22 victory over New Zealand in front of the biggest Test crowd in 50 years, surpassing the previous benchmark set in 1974.

Now, the two men's teams will meet once again to decide who will be world champions. And in the women's tournament, the same showdown will decide who is on top.

Australia and New Zealand have contested the last four women's World Cup finals. In the men's, Australia have cemented their spot as ever with New Zealand returning to the final for the first time since 2013.

New Zealand's men's side have won the World Cup just once back in 2008. The women's side have won it on three occasions but not in 18 years, their last glory coming back in 2008 - the last year New Zealand were on top of the world.

Since then, it has been total and utter Australian domination. New Zealand Women head into their fifth final in a row against the Jillaroos. They do not want it to be a fifth loss in a row.

Coming into this Rugby League World Cup, the talk was all about the new contenders, the ones that had been growing and growing and looked like, this time, they could take down the big boys. The talk was all about Tonga and Samoa showing the landscape of rugby league internationally had changed.

Throughout the group stage, they looked primed and their showdown in the final pool round, in which Tonga came away 20-18 victors, seemed to be the marker that they were here for the big win.

In the end, that match between the two nations ultimately became their final of sorts.

Following that, Tonga succumbed to New Zealand and Samoa fell short of Australia in the men's semi-finals. Exciting Samoa Women could not keep up in a 32-0 loss to New Zealand Women.

They edged closer in some respects but could not complete the job.

The task is set for New Zealand's men - do what they did 18 years ago and release Australia's near two-decade long grip on the title.

Kalyn Ponga became the emblem of how the change to State of Origin eligibility would open up the international landscape as he could still play for Queensland but also represent his heritage. He did that valiantly by returning from a broken arm in that opening clash within just 22 days to star in the semi-finals.

What it would mean to him to complete the journey.

The World Cup storyline, for many, was going to be how a nation could defy the odds to win and send shockwaves globally.

While on the face of it New Zealand winning seems normal, it is anything but. They can still change the landscape, mark their moment, move the competition on.

A victory for them means Australia will be denied the chance to say they have been world champions for 20 years - surely that is as good a motivation as any?

One bookend is a win for Australia. Could the other bookend be glory for New Zealand?

articles.title: Wales v New Zealand: Taine Basham starts as Aaron Wainwright ruled out against All Blacks
articles.summary: Wales number eight Taine Basham will start his first international for four years as he replaces the injured Aaron Wainwright against New Zealand.
articles.body:
Wales number eight Taine Basham will start his first international in four years as he replaces the injured Aaron Wainwright for the Nations Championship match against New Zealand on Saturday.

Basham is part of a back-row reshuffle with James Botham starting instead of fellow Cardiff flanker Alex Mann, and Jac Morgan completing the trio.

Wing Josh Adams, who scored two tries in the 28-21 victory against Japan, is left out in favour of Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb who wins only his second cap.

Lock Adam Beard comes in for Ben Carter as head coach Steve Tandy makes four starting changes.

Sale prop Tomas Francis has been ruled out for the rest of the campaign by injury with Cardiff tight-head Keiron Assiratti called into the squad.

Back rower Taine Plumtree and props Gareth Thomas and Dillon Lewis are named among the replacements with Rhys Carre not in the match-day 23.

Llewellyn aims to give Wales a hint of Sonny Bill

Wales prop Francis targets fourth World Cup

Leicester back rower Wainwright has proved Wales’ most effective forward ball-carrier in recent times.

He picked up a minor calf injury against Japan and has spent the week in a protective boot as he battles to be fit against Australia

Basham was recalled to the Wales squad after impressing for Cardiff.

His previous Wales appearance came as a replacement in the 2024 Six Nations against England, while his last international start came in the 2022 tournament against the same opposition.

It is only his second Test start at number eight.

"I'm delighted that Taine gets an opportunity this weekend," said Tandy.

"It's been a while since his last appearance for Wales but he didn't give up and has put in a lot of dedication and hard work to get back.

"The way he's been playing for Cardiff has been great and I'm excited to see him go on Saturday."

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and BBC Radio 5Live

It will be a second cap for Hamer-Webb after he started the Six Nations defeat against Scotland in February.

The 26-year-old wing has been in fine form for his club side having scored a hat-trick against Saracens in the Prem.

Adams, 31, had made only one start for Cardiff before facing Japan where he had a major effect on the game with two tries and a turnover.

Beard, 30, will win his 69th cap after playing for his French club Montpellier last weekend.

Wales are looking to improve the line-out after losing six on their own throw against Japan.

Wales have not beaten New Zealand since 1953 with the All Blacks winning the past 34 matches and scoring more than 50 points on their three previous trips to Cardiff.

Dave Rennie’s side resumed their Nations Championship campaign with an impressive 43-21 victory against Scotland in Edinburgh last weekend.

"We're excited for the opportunity we have against New Zealand," said Tandy.

"It was good to get the win last Saturday, but some elements of our execution weren't where we wanted.

"We have to go up another level this weekend and be more ruthless. We have one of the best teams in the world coming.

"We want to be better and put in an 80-minute performance."

Smiling Rees-Zammit has no fear of All Blacks

Why Wales have a lot to prove despite beating Japan

articles.title: IRL Golden Boot: Rugby League World Cup stars Rob Hawkins, Kalyn Ponga and Stacey Waaka win awards
articles.summary: England's Rob Hawkins wins the International Rugby League's wheelchair Golden Boot award for the third year running.
articles.body:
England's Rob Hawkins has won the International Rugby League's wheelchair Golden Boot award for the third year running.

Hawkins, 25, is the first player in any form of rugby league to win three successive Golden Boots - awarded by the IRL to the best player in the world during the calendar year.

He is only the second player in rugby league history, after Australia and Queensland great Johnathan Thurston, to win a Golden Boot three times.

New Zealand full-back Kalyn Ponga won the men's Golden Boot award and New Zealand's Stacey Waaka the women's.

Hawkins is set to be part of the England team who will seek to retain the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup when they face rivals France in Wollongong, Australia, on Friday at 08:45 GMT.

He saw off competition from England team-mate Joe Coyd, plus France trio Jeremy Bourson, Nicolas Clausells and Dany Denuwelaere, to win the award.

Ireland captain Joe Calcott and Australia's Bayley McKenna and Adam Tannock were also nominated.

Hawkins has scored 19 tries at the World Cup for England, including five as they thrashed Australia 86-28 in Tuesday's semi-final.

England's wheelchair head coach Tom Coyd said: "I am so proud of Rob. His consistency comes from his humility and how grounded he is. He never stops pushing forward and is an inspiration to his team-mates and to me."

Ponga, 28, produced a starring performance in New Zealand's 34-10 semi-final win over Tonga on Saturday - only 23 days after breaking his forearm.

He also shone in last month's NRL Grand Final, despite being on the losing side as Newcastle Knights were beaten 19-18 by Sydney Roosters.

Dual-code international Waaka, 31, scored a hat-trick in New Zealand's 32-0 semi-final victory over Samoa.

Waaka won a bronze medal in rugby union at the 2025 World Cup to go with two Olympic golds and a Commonwealth Games title in sevens.

The award winners were announced in Brisbane, with several greats of the game selected as inaugural inductees into the IRL Hall of Legends.

They included Sir Billy Boston - the first rugby league player to be knighted - Ellery Hanley, Malcolm Reilly, Alex Murphy, Neil Fox, Roger Millward and Mick Sullivan, the only Englishman to have won two World Cups.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Tadhg Beirne captains strong Ireland selection vs Fiji as Jamison Gibson-Park returns, Rob Baloucoune passed fit
articles.summary: Andy Farrell's Ireland host Fiji at Aviva Stadium, Dublin on Saturday in Nations Championship (8.10pm); team selection shows seven changes to thumping win vs Argentina as Jamison Gibson-Park, Tommy O'Brien, Bundee Aki, Jamie Osborne, Ronan Kelleher, James Ryan, Josh van der Flier come in
articles.body:
Two of those changes are enforced as hooker Dan Sheehan (concussion) and No 8 Sean Jansen (knee) were ruled out, but several other injury concerns have been allayed.

Indeed, wing Rob Baloucoune is fit to start again, as is Mack Hansen despite an ankle knock - the latter shifting to full-back with Hugo Keenan rested and Tommy O'Brien brought into the back-three.

Josh van der Flier is also fit despite his own ankle complaint, starting at openside flanker with Nick Timoney shifting to No 8 in the absence of Jansen, Jack Conan and Caelan Doris due to injury.

Experienced scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park returns to the starting XV, with Craig Casey dropping down to the bench.

Elsewhere, there is a new-look midfield with Jamie Osborne and Bundee Aki starting at centre. Stuart McCloskey moves to the bench, while Robbie Henshaw drops out of the matchday squad.

Sam Prendergast partners Gibson-Park at half-back, while Ronan Kelleher replaces Sheehan at hooker to form a front-row alongside Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong.

James Ryan is promoted from the bench to start in place of the rested Joe McCarthy, with Ryan Baird completing the back-row alongside Van der Flier and Timoney.

articles.title: Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup final: England v France to be live on BBC iPlayer
articles.summary: England's bid to retain the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup will be shown live on the BBC on Friday.
articles.body:
England's bid to retain the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup will be shown live and free-to-air on the BBC on Friday.

The final against great rivals France, in Wollongong, Australia, kicks off at 08:45 GMT, and will be broadcast on BBC iPlayer.

England defeated France 28-24, with a dramatic late Tom Halliwell try, to win the last Wheelchair World Cup in Manchester in November 2022.

And the two teams have a history of tight, action-packed matches - having contested the past three finals: France winning 42-40 in Gillingham in 2013, and then 38-34 in Perpignan in 2017.

England head coach Tom Coyd said: "To be flying the flag for England at this late stage of the Rugby League World Cup is an honour for us and we hope we can keep doing the country proud on Friday."

Alongside the live stream, fans can follow the action through BBC Sport's live text coverage, available across the BBC Sport website and app.

BBC Radio 5 Live will also have live coverage of the men's and women's finals on Sunday as the tournament reaches its conclusion in Brisbane, with Australia and New Zealand going head-to-head in both matches.

The BBC Sport website and app will have live text coverage for both the men's and women's finals, and will have digital clip highlights online later on Sunday.

Alex Kay-Jelski, director of BBC Sport, said: "Sport is at its very best when it gives audiences moments they can share, and an England team playing in a World Cup final is exactly that.

"Bringing audiences the biggest homegrown sporting moments is at the heart of BBC Sport, and we're proud to bring rugby fans England's final with France for the world title on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app."

Watch live on BBC iPlayer, as well as the BBC Sport website and app, which will also have live text coverage

Wheelchair rugby league was developed in France as a way of bringing the sport to people with disabilities. It is fully inclusive, with disabled and non-disabled players able to play on the same team, and follows many of the same conventions as the running game.

Teams of five players have six tackles to score. Tackles on the ball carrier are made by pulling off a tag attached to each player's shirt. A try scores four points, with two points for penalties and conversions, which are taken by punching the ball off a tee over the posts.

The game is played with an oval ball and lasts for 80 minutes, with a maximum of two non-disabled and three disabled players allowed on the field at any one time.

It differs in several ways from wheelchair rugby - which is played at the Paralympics. Wheelchair rugby features a round ball and teams of four, has no conversions, and no tackling is allowed (but it is a full-contact sport, allowing collisions between players): Teams instead must dribble or pass the ball every 10 seconds.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Henry Pollock, Max Ojomoh, Will Joseph start for England vs Japan as part of 10 changes

articles.body:
Fresh from his two-try impact off the bench - out of position on the wing - Pollock is named to start at No 8 by head coach Steve Borthwick. Despite his huge impact to date, Saturday will only be the second time in 15 Tests Pollock starts.

Ojomoh comes in for his first cap in a year to start at inside-centre with Seb Atkinson out injured (hip), while Joseph replaces Tommy Freeman on the right wing in his first England appearance since July 2022.

Elsewhere, there are three new starters in the front-row with loosehead Ellis Genge, hooker Luke Cowan-Dickie and tighthead Asher Opoku-Fordjour.

George Martin starts in the second row, while experienced fly-half George Ford is picked ahead of Marcus Smith.

Wing Cadan Murley and full-back Freddie Steward form a new back-three with Joseph, in the absence of injured duo Immanuel Feyi-Waboso (ankle) and George Furbank (groin).

Outside-centre Henry Slade and scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet maintain their places in the backline, with Maro Itoje captaining the side once again from the second-row.

There are positional switches for Alex Coles - lock to blindside flanker - and Ben Earl - No 8 to openside flanker.

Northampton Saints scrum-half Archie McParland is also in line to make his Test debut off the replacements bench.

Hooker Theo Dan, loosehead Emmanuel Iyogun, tighthead Joe Heyes, lock Arthur Clark and back-rows Ben Curry and Greg Fisilau complete the bench alongside half-backs McParland and Smith.

"Japan are a very well-coached side who will challenge us in different ways, and we know we'll need to bring intensity throughout the game," said Borthwick.

"The atmosphere at Allianz Stadium last week was incredible. The players really fed off the energy in the stadium, and we're really looking forward to being back on Saturday.

"We're all delighted for Archie. He's had some bad luck with injury, so it's especially pleasing to be able to name him in an England matchday 23 for the first time. He's an outstanding young talent who has worked hard to get to this point, and we're all excited to see how he goes."

articles.title: England v Japan: Henry Pollock, Max Ojomoh and Will Joseph start
articles.summary: Free-scoring back row Henry Pollock will make only his second start for England in Saturday's Nations Championship meeting with Japan.
articles.body:
Free-scoring back row Henry Pollock will make only his second start for England after being named at number eight in a much-changed side for Saturday's Nations Championship meeting with Japan.

Despite mainly being restricted to the bench, Pollock has scored eight tries in 14 Tests, including a double as a stand-in wing against Australia on Sunday.

After man-of-the-match performances in Northampton's run to the Prem title, the 21-year-old will get a chance to press his claim to a Test starting spot.

Elsewhere in-form Will Joseph, whose only previous England cap came under now-Japan coach Eddie Jones in 2022, is given his chance in the absence of injured wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso.

Max Ojomoh comes in at inside centre in a remarkable return to favour.

The 26-year-old has not played for England since starring in the win over Argentina a year ago and was not initially part of England's 36-strong squad for this month's matches.

With his contract at Bath up for renewal at the end of the season, he has been linked with a move to the Top 14 in the French press.

However, a stellar performance in England A's win over an Argentina XV last Friday has earned Ojomoh promotion into the senior starting line-up ahead of Fraser Dingwall, with first choice Seb Atkinson ruled out with a hip injury.

George Ford is named at fly-half with Fin Smith, who recovered from a calf injury to play 80 minutes against the Wallabies, rotated out of the matchday squad and Marcus Smith, who has impressed in recent weeks with Harlequins, on the bench.

Cadan Murley comes into the back three with Tommy Freeman left out, while there is an all-new starting front row of Ellis Genge, Luke Cowan-Dickie and Asher Opoku-Fordjour.

Northampton scrum-half Archie McParland is poised to make his debut off the bench, with Greg Fisilau, Arthur Clark and Emmanuel Iyogun, who all have one cap, alongside him in an inexperienced set of replacements.

Live on BBC Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website and app

England's Mitchell could miss Six Nations after hamstring operation

Lawes recovering after hospital stay with infection

Japan want 'the sky to fall in' at Twickenham - Jones

Enforced absences have prevented England from building on last weekend's win with a similar selection.

Only centre Henry Slade, scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet and captain Maro Itoje have retained their starting spot in the same position.

The rejig, however, gives others a chance to make their case a year out from the Rugby World Cup in Australia.

While Pollock has made regular try-scoring second-half cameos in his England career so far, the 21-year-old's only previous start was in February's dismal 42-21 home defeat by Ireland.

England were routed at the breakdown that day and Pollock's challenge, albeit against weaker opposition, will be to prove his effectiveness in close quarters, as well as in open spaces.

Pollock had Ben Earl and Tom Curry alongside him against Ireland, and Borthwick has brought more ballast into the back-row blend on this occasion with Alex Coles moved to blind-side flanker in place of the injured Ollie Chessum.

Like Pollock, Ojomoh knows that head coach Steve Borthwick will be focused on small details, as much as showreel highlights.

The Bath star's silky playmaking skills and running threat have never been in doubt, but England have wanted more from the Bath star in defence and his work off the ball.

However, if, as expected, England secure the majority of possession, Ojomoh's ability to pick passes in the face of a defence could spring his backline.

Joseph, whose older brother Jonathan won 54 caps for England between 2012 and 2020, has been one of the stars of Gloucester's resurgence this season, alternating between wing and midfield.

England have won all six previous Tests against Japan, most recently running out 52-17 winners in Tokyo in June 2024.

Replacements: Dan, Iyogun, Heyes, Clark, Curry, Fisilau, McParland, M Smith

One minute, four years ago - Joseph's long wait is up

Joseph was taken on England's 2022 tour of Australia by Jones as a teenage apprentice player, alongside fellow London Irish academy product Henry Arundell.

While Arundell's try-scoring cameo in the first Test captured most of the attention, Joseph also made his international bow, coming on for the final minute of the team's second-Test win in place of Guy Porter.

Now 24, it has been a long wait for his next piece of international experience.

"Being back here is quite strange, it feels a little deja-vu," Joseph told Rugby Union Weekly last month about his return to the England camp.

"I feel a lot like a new player, even though I have been here before and know a lot of the lads, but I am just really excited to showcase what I can do."

Since making his last England appearance Joseph has lost the hearing in his left ear as a result of an auto-immune disease.

"I was in a training session, the whistle went and my ear felt a bit funny," he remembered.

"Then we had a swimming session and when I got out the pool I couldn't hear out of my left ear.

"My understanding is that my body over-reacted to something that was going on in my ear and shut down the nerves that allow me to hear. It was scary. It was tough.

"When you have only got one ear [that works] your surroundings are all off. I feel like I have adapted now and got used to playing with one ear, but at the start I wasn't sure whether I was going to be able to do it."

articles.body:
Ulster's James McNabney is poised to make his Ireland debut off the bench as head coach Andy Farrell makes seven changes for Saturday's Nations Championship match against Fiji.

In addition to a raft of personnel changes, Farrell has made two key positional switches with Nick Timoney and Mack Hansen moving to number eight and full-back.

Timoney's switch comes amid an injury crisis at number eight, with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen all ruled out through injury, while Hansen replaces Hugo Keenan, who drops out of the squad after scoring a hat-trick of tries in the 42-12 win over Argentina.

Jamie Osborne, Bundee Aki, Tommy O'Brien and Jamison Gibson-Park are also drafted into the backline, with Rob Baloucoune and Sam Prendergast retained.

With back-to-back world champions South Africa bringing their much-vaunted scrum power to Dublin next week, Farrell has opted to stick with first-choice props Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong.

Behind an experienced second row of Ryan and Beirne, Ryan Baird keeps his place at blind-side flanker after impressing on his return against Argentina, while Timoney is entrusted with a first Test start at number eight after an eye-catching showing at open-side last week.

Full-back Beauden Barrett will captain New Zealand for the first time when he leads out the All Blacks for the Nations Championship game against Wales in Cardiff on Saturday.

articles.title: Rugby Union: Courtney Lawes staph infection led to 10-day hospital stay
articles.summary: Courtney Lawes says he spent 10 days in hospital after doctors found his infection markers were "through the roof" as he battled a serious illness.
articles.body:
Courtney Lawes has revealed he spent 10 days in hospital after doctors found his infection markers were "through the roof" as he battled a serious illness.

The 37-year-old said a staph infection , external was the reason for his absence from rugby, having not played since Sale Sharks' Champions Cup defeat by Glasgow Warriors on 17 October.

Speaking on The Good, The Bad & The Rugby Xtra podcast, , external Lawes said he initially believed he was suffering from flu.

"I had flu symptoms but some really bad muscle pains with it. On the way home, my right arm basically stopped working, so really weird symptoms," Lawes said.

A staph infection is caused by staphylococcus bacteria, which can live harmlessly on the skin but become serious if they enter the bloodstream through a wound or break in the skin.

Lawes said he believes the infection may have entered his body through a foot injury sustained during a match.

"It ripped up my feet, and it didn't heal very well, so I think it's from that," he explained.

Lawes said he sought advice from the medical staff at Sale Sharks, who initially planned for a doctor to assess him the following day.

However, his condition continued to deteriorate.

"I continued to get worse, was running a really high temperature.

"My right arm didn't work, my abductors and pelvis were completely locked off as well. My left arm was functional and that was about it."

The former England and British & Irish Lions forward said his wife, Jessica, urged him to attend an accident and emergency department.

Lawes described the wait for the results from blood tests as one of the "darkest places" he had ever been in, before doctors informed him his infection markers were dangerously high and admitted him to hospital.

Four days into his hospital stay, Lawes was diagnosed with a staph infection.

Initially treated with penicillin via an IV drip, his temperature remained high and his infection markers continued to rise until doctors identified the source of the illness and prescribed the correct antibiotics.

"In the first six days in hospital it was proper dark. The pain in my muscles was like nothing I've ever had before.

"I don't know how you measure pain but in those first five days that was the most pain I've ever tolerated."

Lawes said he was warned that untreated bloodstream infections can spread to vital organs and have potentially life-threatening consequences.

The England international, who has won more than 100 caps for his country, is now on the road to recovery.

"I'm obviously feeling better, still recovering but we'll just take it day by day," he said.

articles.title: Wales vs New Zealand: How Steve Tandy is over-relying on scrum-half Tomos Williams
articles.summary: Wales head coach Steve Tandy says is a big demand on the workload of scrum-half Tomos Williams.
articles.body:
Wales head coach Steve Tandy says there has been a big demand on the workload of scrum-half Tomos Williams.

The British and Irish Lions number nine again played the full 80 minutes in the 28-21 defeat of Japan with Rebuen Morgan-Williams an unused replacement.

Williams has started 12 out of 13 Test matches in the Tandy era and has completed five of those games.

"It is a big balance to strike," said Tandy as he prepared his side to face New Zealand in Cardiff on Saturday.

"When one of your best players, a British and Irish Lion, is in that position, there probably is an over-demand on Tomos."

Williams dominates scrum-half minutes in Tandy era

The only game Williams has not started in the Tandy era was the 73-0 hammering inflicted by South Africa in November 2025.

That match fell outside World Rugby's international window with England-based club players not eligible for the fixture.

In those 12 internationals Williams has started, Tandy has used the replacement scrum-half for just 48 minutes with an average of four minutes per game.

Williams has playing a full 80 minutes on five occasions with his average minutes per Test at 74.3 minutes, although that includes two yellow cards he has picked up.

The players chosen as bench cover for Williams have played a combined total of only 30 minutes in the past nine Tests in 2026 with Williams starting all the games and completing four of them.

"There is a massive reliance on Tomos, you can't run away from that," said Tandy.

"Most teams are reliant on big players and Tomos loves playing. If you look at getting a rhythm, Tomos loves playing rugby.

"Being taken off, not that it is an issue, but at Saracens, it's probably more of a rotation policy.

"Some boys like being in the groove, while some can handle that rotation policy. But at the minute, he's in a great space."

Kieran Hardy had been Williams' under-utilised deputy until he picked up a serious knee injury in October that could rule him out of the 2027 World Cup in Australia.

Morgan-Williams and uncapped Dragons scrum-half Che Hope are the other scrum-halves in the autumn squad.

"Reuben is doing well and Che is an exciting young talent," said Tandy.

"It's just making sure we feel we manage that bit correctly so we are doing it right for that person, as well as Tomos.

"There is no substitute for Test rugby, but you've also got to do right by them, with who you're playing against.

"So potentially putting Che in to start against New Zealand, those are the things we, as coaches, take into consideration. We know we need to grow that space."

articles.title: History of Wales v All Blacks: Seven decades of cheating, scandal and drama
articles.summary: It is more than 70 years since Wales last beat New Zealand but the fixture has rarely failed to deliver drama.
articles.body:
Cheating, national scandal, timekeeping disasters and spine-tingling drama... Wales against New Zealand rarely disappoints.

The history of matches between two nations that bleed rugby - and plenty of the red stuff has been spilled over the years - is almost a history of the game itself.

Since the 1905 'Match of the Century' which gave rise to the tradition of singing national anthems before sports events, they have battled.

Wales may have won three of the first four meetings but since success in 1953 the lengthening losing run has hung like a millstone around the necks of generations of players.

Gareth Edwards, Barry John, JPR Williams, Jonathan Davies, Shane Williams and Alun Wyn Jones all tried with Wales and failed.

There is bitterness that the wait has gone on so long - more than 70 years - not least after one of the most talked about accusations of cheating in rugby history.

Cardiff in 1978 hosted what was as close to a World Cup final as the time allowed. The All Blacks had defeated the British & Irish Lions the previous year and Wales were Grand Slam champions.

It was the first time New Zealand had visited Cardiff since the infamous late-night incident after which Keith Murdoch was sent home in disgrace after punching a hotel doorman. Still today, All Blacks players, staff and fans stop at the Angel Hotel, opposite the Principality Stadium on Westgate Street, for a commemorative pint.

In 1978, Graham Mourie's tourists scored the game's only try but Wales had dominated, leading 12-10 as the clock inside the cauldron of the old Arms Park ticked towards the final minute.

Little did they know that New Zealand's players, braced for their biggest challenge of the tour, had hatched an escape plan the previous night.

Andy Haden, the All Blacks lock and culprit in chief, later wrote: "With Wales in front, I knew there could only be a minute or so left. I went to Frank Oliver, my locking partner... and told him the plan in four words: 'I'm going to dive'."

Sure enough, Haden catapulted out of the line-out just as Wales hooker Bobby Windsor threw the ball.

Wales' players stood bemused as referee Roger Quittenton of England gave a penalty and Brian McKechnie landed the winning points.

Quittenton would later claim he had penalised Geoff Wheel for an infringement, but the Kiwi intent was clear and the apparent injustice would rankle.

Windsor described the game as the worst day of his career. He added: "I knew straight away that it was a con job. When we found out later that they had planned it the night before, that really got to me. I'll never forget that as long as I live."

It would be 26 years until Wales would come as close to ending the losing run.

In contrast to 1978, few expected much of a young Wales side in 2004 that had done little to impress despite scoring a record 37 points against the All Blacks in defeat at the World Cup in Australia the previous year.

Under new head coach Mike Ruddock and with a rising young star, Gavin Henson, in their ranks, Wales played with abandon and led at half-time through tries by Tom Shanklin and Mefin Davies.

New Zealand, jolted into action, had Joe Rokocoko, the most potent player on the planet at the time, to thank for two wonderful solo tries. But for once, Wales refused to yield and could have pulled off a shock if not for some disastrous timekeeping.

Wales, back to within a point after Henson's kick, thought there was injury time to come on the stadium clock, which in fact showed the correct time on the referee's watch.

With seconds to go, Stephen Jones kicked the ball away and Wales never had another chance.

Try-scorer Shanklin said: "It's actually more painful and frustrating now, when I look back, than it was at the time. We had been through some tough years so I was actually quite pleased that we hadn't been hammered and put on a great show.

"But looking back, you realise now just how close we came to making history. However, the pay-off was that autumn campaign set us up for another piece of history with the Grand Slam the following year."

Just how to respond to the Haka has troubled opposition throughout the history of the game.

In 1905, the Welsh crowd's singing of Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau as a response to the Haka was the first time a national anthem was sung before an international sports event.

It had the desired effect. The New Zealand captain Dave Gallaher wrote later that he had never experienced anything like it in his life and they lost the only game in their 35-match tour.

However a century later, the Welsh Rugby Union's (WRU) attempted response to the Haka backfired disastrously.

In 2005, the WRU asked to play the anthem after the Haka as part of the centenary celebrations of the fixture. New Zealand agreed - as a one-off.

So when the WRU asked to do the same again a year later, the All Blacks were not impressed. Both sides dug in their heels, and 74,000 expectant fans inside what was then the Millennium Stadium, as well as the Welsh players, looked on perplexed as a recording of the All Blacks performing the Haka in their dressing room was shown on the stadium's giant screens.

"Playing against them in 2006 will always stick with me," said former prop , external Adam Jones.

"For some reason the powers that be decided that it would be a good idea to try and convince the All Blacks to do their Haka before we responded with our national anthem.

"They put 40-odd points on us that day, and [then Harlequins team-mate] Nick Evans told me the incident ensured they wanted to destroy us."

Having learned from the experience, Wales two years later conjured up a spine-tingling response that remains etched in the mind of every spectator.

Wales stare down All Blacks haka. Video, 00:02:33 Wales stare down All Blacks haka

It was Warren Gatland's first game in charge of Wales against his native New Zealand and he challenged his senior players to understand the significance of the traditional Maori challenge. It was Martyn Williams who came up with a wonderfully simple but devilishly clever response.

"Gats explained that if you turn first, then psychologically the All Blacks have already got one up on you," said the former flanker.

"It was a bit of a throw-away comment, but I asked, 'well what if we just don't turn around?'. Let's line up on the 10-metre line, so we're not preventing the kick-off, and we'll just stand there."

What followed was 80 seconds of sporting theatre that was proof that rugby does not need pyrotechnics or piped music, just a stony-faced display of sheer determination.

Wales had positioned themselves perfectly, so it was the All Blacks, who had massed on the halfway line, who were forced to retreat.

"It felt like we were there forever and it just got louder and louder the longer we stood there," recalled Williams.

"It's one of those moments that everyone remembers. It was great theatre and, actually, the New Zealand boys said afterwards they loved it as well."

This weekend, it is Steve Tandy's side who will have to face the All Blacks and their Haka.

Few observers expect them to bring to an end the long wait for a win - but if they do it will doubtless add yet more sporting drama to a fixture already rich in history and infamy.

articles.title: Nations Championship: England, Ireland in points race, return of Eddie Jones to Twickenham, injury-hit France face Springboks
articles.summary: Second week of Nations Championship Tests in northern hemisphere sees England host Japan as Eddie Jones returns to Twickenham; Ireland welcome Fiji; injury-hit France vs Springboks in blockbuster; inaugural tournament concludes at Allianz Stadium from November 27-29
articles.body:
Heading into the fifth weekend of six Nations Championship rounds - split between July in the southern hemisphere and November in Europe - England and Ireland have near-identical records.

Even with bonus points in play, Steve Borthwick's side and Andy Farrell's Ireland are set for a close finish, with their final standings potentially determining who reaches the title decider.

Both currently sit on 15 competition points, but England are 42 points better off in terms of points difference at the moment, owing to the fact they beat Fiji 73-8 in July, and added to that with a handsome 45-22 home success over Australia last week.

In July, Ireland edged a high-scoring win over Australia to claim a bonus point, followed it up with another bonus-point victory over Japan (despite winning by just 16 points), before losing to the All Blacks at Eden Park without securing a bonus point for either a narrow defeat or scoring four tries

On home soil, Ireland then dispatched of Argentina 42-12 last week , but failed to score a point in the final quarter of the Test, which they may yet pay for.

For England, they lost to South Africa at Ellis Park without banking any losing bonus points, then annihilated Fiji in Liverpool and held on to win in Argentina with a crucial bonus point.

Last week's morale-boosting win over Australia has now given England a great chance of at least finishing second and facing one of South Africa or New Zealand on finals weekend at Twickenham.

For Ireland to overtake England, they must outperform them across the final two rounds. That means beating South Africa in Dublin while hoping New Zealand defeat England at Twickenham, or securing more bonus points in defeat to the Springboks than England manage against the All Blacks.

With comfortable wins expected for England and Ireland against Japan and Fiji respectively this Saturday, the Irish are unlikely to make significant inroads into England's substantial points-difference advantage.

Instead, it is likely to come down to bonus points.

Jones stoking the flames on his return as Japan seek huge shock

Former England head coach Eddie Jones is plotting a historic upset, backing Japan to stun England at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

The Brave Blossoms have lost all six previous Tests against England and are 40-1 outsiders to pull off a seismic Nations Championship shock.

But Jones, who coached England from 2016 to 2022, is preparing a few surprises for his former side.

"It's a big week for Japanese rugby," Jones said this week. "We realise England are a nation we've never been able to beat.

"Everyone knows the record and we want to do something a bit different this week and we've trained like that, so I'm really pleased with the team.

"We've had really good training to prepare us for the game we are expecting against England.

"We had two days of very settled and pretty training but Wednesday was quite dirty. We had to adapt to certain situations and in the end we did it really well.

"I was really pleased with the players, really pleased with their effort, really pleased with the way they adapted to the situations.

"I'm looking forward to going to Twickenham with this young Japanese team that's going to play the house down."

Jones remains England's most successful coach by win rate, with 72 per cent, having won two Six Nations titles, including the 2016 Grand Slam. He also guided England to the 2019 World Cup final, but his tenure ended acrimoniously, with his side booed by fans in 2022.

"If you look at the stats, they stand the test of time," Jones said. "So there's no reason why I shouldn't be pleased to go back to Twickenham."

The 66-year-old has been doing the media rounds this week, also saying his Japan side are aiming to "make the Twickenham sky fall in on" Steve Borthwick's "distracted" charges in Saturday's Test.

Injury-hit France welcome Springboks to Paris in blockbuster

Two of the world's top sides go head-to-head on Friday as France host South Africa.

The Springboks insist they have no special plans to contain Antoine Dupont at fly-half, instead trusting their defence to limit the space available to the French playmaker.

With Romain Ntamack injured and Matthieu Jalibert already ruled out, Dupont will wear the No 10 jersey, with Maxime Lucu at scrum-half.

Both are more accustomed to playing at nine but have featured at fly-half for their clubs, and South Africa expect the pair to interchange positions during the match.

"He's [Dupont] played at 10 before for his ​club [Toulouse], and we saw the game where he played there. He was very good," captain Siya Kolisi told reporters on Thursday.

"I mean, he can play almost anywhere ​on the field, so I don't think it is a surprise to ⁠see him there.

"Obviously, nobody wants injuries, ⁠but every team experiences them and you have to adjust. He's a good enough player to do it. He's shown ‌that over the years."

Kolisi said the Springboks had no specific plan to stop Dupont at fly-half, insisting their defence would stick to its usual system regardless of the opposition or individuals they face.

"Our system doesn't change for any team we play against. We have a system that works and we've prepared for them," he added.

"We haven't done anything special for him individually just because he's ⁠playing at 10. We know Lucu has also played ​at 10 for Bordeaux, so it will be natural for ​them to swap positions.

"We know Antoine wants to be on ​the ball a lot and creates a lot, so for him to move ⁠to nine [during the game)] will also be natural."

Kolisi expects an intense atmosphere in Paris, the scene of the Springboks' epic 29-28 victory over France in the quarter-finals of ⁠the 2023 Rugby World Cup.

South Africa have ​won nine of their last 10 Tests against the French, the only ​blemish a 30-26 loss in Marseille in 2022.

They are unbeaten in their last five Tests in Paris, last losing in ‌the French capital in 2005.

articles.title: Wales v New Zealand: All Blacks target Jac Morgan in Nations Championship match
articles.summary: New Zealand coach Dave Rennie says they have spoken about targeting Wales' Lions flanker Jac Morgan in the Nations Championship encounter.
articles.body:
New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie says they have spoken about eliminating the breakdown threat of Wales flanker Jac Morgan in the Nations Championship match in Cardiff on Saturday.

The All Blacks are firm favourites to extend their 73-year winning run against Wales this weekend.

But New Zealand have identified Morgan’s contact area work as one of Wales’ main strengths.

"When [Wales] chop tackle, you've got guys like Morgan who are excellent on the ball," said Rennie.

"So we're well aware of that and we'll have a focus on eliminating him before he can cause us stress, because that is a big part of their game."

Basham starts for Wales as Wainwright ruled out

Full-back Barrett leads New Zealand for first time

How and why Wales are relying on scrum-half Williams

Rennie highlighted other issues that concern him about Wales.

"Their line-out has been excellent during the last year," he said, even though Steve Tandy's side saw six of their throws go astray last weekend.

"Maybe it was not quite as accurate against Japan but up until then, it's been top-notch," the veteran coach added.

"They're also prepared to play and, in Tomos Williams, they have one of the best nines in the world.

"We've got to make sure we don't let him have too much space, because he's got such a high-quality kicking game and kicks off both feet.

"They've got a number of players that if we give them time and space, they'll be a handful.

"They have a big midfield and absolute jets on the wing, so we know a fair bit about the enemy."

Rennie has made eight starting changes from the side that defeated Scotland 43-21.

Sections of the New Zealand media say that selection reflects the lack of threat Wales pose, as the 10th-ranked side in the world face the second, but Rennie does not subscribe to that view.

"Wales will be pretty fired up to put in a quality performance," he said.

"So we've picked a strong side we think will show the respect for them."

Rennie is also familiar with many of the Wales coaching staff.

He was Glasgow coach between 2017 and 2020 when Wales duo Tandy and Danny Wilson were part of Gregor Townsend's Scotland backroom staff.

Wales defence coach Peter Murchie was also part of Rennie's backroom team at Kobelco Kobe Steelers in Japan before linking up with Tandy in the Welsh set-up.

"I know them well and they are very good, smart coaches," said Rennie.

"Pete did a phenomenal job defensively with us at Kobe, and I can see the impact he's having already. And likewise with Steve.

"It's going to take time to turn things around, but I can definitely see the impact they're having."

Rennie has bittersweet memories of coaching an international side against Wales at the Principality Stadium, when he was leading Australia in December 2022.

He masterminded a wonderful Wallabies comeback as Wales led 34-13 before the tourists scored 26 unanswered points to win 39-34.

It proved to be Rennie's final action as Australia coach. He was replaced by Eddie Jones, while the Wales boss that day, Wayne Pivac, was dismissed with Warren Gatland returning.

Rennie remembers the atmosphere that day.

"It is one of the great grounds in world rugby, with the roof on, the national anthems you've got to soak it up and enjoy it," he said.

"It can be pretty daunting, but it's special.

"We'll definitely embrace that and all the boys are excited to be here."

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and BBC Radio 5Live.

All Blacks look to continue seven decades of dominance

New Zealand have won the past 34 Tests against Wales in a winning sequence that stretches back to 1953, with the All Blacks scoring more than 50 points on each of their three previous visits to Cardiff over the past five years.

New Zealand and South Africa are currently unbeaten in the southern hemisphere table, competing for top spot before the Nations Championship play-off weekend at the end of the month.

Rennie, however, says his side are not concentrating on trying to close the points-difference gap on the Springboks.

"It's just a Test match and our focus is this week," he insisted.

"We'll probably be looking at things going into the last game, where it might be a little bit clearer around what we need to do.

"I think South Africa are about 70 points clear, so if we end up on the same amount of points, it's unlikely we'd catch them.

"There's a real danger to go out and think you need to score X amount of points, you end up overplaying and getting embarrassed.

"We've got a clear plan around how we want to play and whatever happens, happens."

articles.title: Nations Championship: How the driving maul became a try machine
articles.summary: A kick to the corner is now a no-brainer for captains, with the driving maul a more potent weapon than ever.
articles.body:
Back in March, leading Italy by two points and with a penalty just outside their 22m, England captain Maro Itoje pulled rank.

"Don't argue with me, take the three!" he told fly-half Fin Smith. Who duly did.

It is an age-old tactical call: kick or twist? Whether to call for the tee, go for the posts and a likely three points, or aim for touch, an attacking line-out and five or, potentially, seven.

Chris Robshaw, one of Itoje's predecessors, was haunted by those decisions.

A clutch of them turned out badly under him, most memorably when England chased possible victory, rather than taking on a potentially match-tying kick, as they trailed Wales 28-25 late on in a 2015 Rugby World Cup pool game.

Across six Nations Championship matches last weekend, teams opted for goal just three times. Instead, the corner called on almost every occasion.

The change in mentality reflects shifting probabilities. The line-out odds are no longer so long. There is a run on driving-maul tries across the game.

Analysis from stats company Oval Insights comparing the past seven seasons of November Test rugby and the English top flight, show that mauls are delivering tries more consistently than at any point since they began collecting the metric.

Rugby's regulations were tweaked in the summer, , external so that defending players can no longer 'swim' up the side of the maul. Previously, so long as they maintained their bind, individuals could work their way round, pulling apart the attacking team's momentum and threatening to steal possession.

Now, once defenders are past the ball and no longer in a position to push, they have to detach and rejoin from behind the back foot.

England forward Alex Coles says the change has made the set-piece stakes higher and more immediate.

"The maul now is so much about who wins that first second," he told BBC Sport.

"Under the old laws, there was more of a chance for a defence to try to rescue and recover the situation.

"Now, essentially, that opportunity to swarm up the side and make it a mess from behind has gone.

"The law change hasn't completely changed it, but it has shifted the balance towards the attack."

As the maul has become a more reliable route to the line, more attack coaches are heading that way.

Maul tries are more than twice as common in this November window than the last, with 0.67 per game compared to 0.3 in 2025.

The story in the Prem is similar. There have been 0.42 per game this season, compared to 0.23 over the opening five rounds of last.

"I'd be interested to know the stats, but I feel like there's more aerial competition now," says Coles.

"Teams are going harder after that because if you can win the ball back at source, it makes such a difference."

Alternatively, if you don't go up in the line-out, you have to win the ground war.

"You can stay down and try to beat them to that punch with your speed and physicality," says Coles.

"If you get them going backwards immediately, then the referees are likely to get the ball moving or you can try and find some seams and break up the setup, make it look a bit more messy through that, rather than swarming around the sides.

"I think we'll see that balance shift back towards more of a 50-50 as teams evolve."

The ripples from the law change reach other parts of the pitch.

The heightened threat of a pushover try can open up space on the opposite wing.

New Zealand's Beauden Barrett had a stroll in for his second try in the win over Scotland last weekend as the hosts, admittedly a man down, were caught horribly narrow.

The premium on discipline, always high, has risen another notch. Concede a penalty on halfway and you are rolling out the red carpet into the red zone.

Whether encouraging a tactic that, to the casual fan at least, is a relatively unspectacular try-scoring method, a year out from a World Cup is the best move by the game's authorities is another question.

It isn't one that Test coaches will be concerning themselves with though.

Calculating the new threats and opportunities and their best chance of landing the biggest prize is where they show their worth.

England made hay in 2025 with tactics and personnel designed to exploit a change in the kick-chase laws, outlawing defences running blocking lines and opening up the aerial contest.

With Jamie George and Maro Itoje's decade-plus club-country partnership and head coach Steve Borthwick's previous specialism in the set-piece, there is a formidable line-out brains trust in camp. Their Red Roses counterparts have long had a formidable driving maul as their calling card as well.

Live on BBC Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website and app

This Saturday against Japan, England will doubtless want a continuation of the expansive display that did for Australia last weekend.

But over the next year, the spotlight may shine just as much on the dark depths of the driving maul.

articles.title: England v Japan: Max Ojomoh must marry talent and toughness - Steve Borthwick
articles.summary: Max Ojomoh must bring physicality, as well as his usual stardust, to England's backline, says head coach Steve Borthwick.
articles.body:
Centre Max Ojomoh - labelled "one of the most talented players in English rugby" - has been challenged to produce a relentless and physical performance against Japan on Saturday.

The Bath man burst on to the international scene in a man-of-the-match display against Argentina at the end of 2025, but has not played for his country in the 12 months since.

Ojomoh was initially left out of Steve Borthwick's wider training squad but after starring for the 'A' team has been catapulted back into the England number 12 shirt and with it World Cup contention.

"Max is one of the most talented players in English rugby," boss Steve Borthwick told BBC Sport.

"His ability to see space and distribute, to hide where he is going to pass and to pass short or long, that's a rare skill."

However Borthwick says the position of centre has changed markedly over the years, and it now requires a level of unyielding physical output to go with a wide skill-set.

"You have to be incredibly skilled in that position, but it demands a skill and toughness it previously probably didn't," he explained.

"It used to be a second receiver, that second pair of eyes, the distribution skills and the potential kicking skills.

"Now they've got to hit and they've got to run in attack and they've got to run in defence, and our centres are involved in a lot of rucks in wider channels.

"Can they get the ball back? And can they tackle with impact to get the ball back? So when I'm talking about centres, I want the incredible skill and I want the incredible toughness.

"And I am full of belief that Max will go and deliver that this weekend."

Two-cap Ojomoh will line up alongside cap centurion George Ford, who returns to the number 10 shirt for the first time since the Six Nations.

Speaking in depth to the Rugby Union Weekly podcast , Ford says one of his main jobs against the Blossoms is to get England's best athletes on the ball as much as possible.

"You can pick attack to pieces at times and say, 'I want this running line and I want you to stand here', but, essentially, if you're getting the ball in Tommy Freeman's hands and Manny Feyi-Waboso's hands and Will Joseph's hands and Cadan Murley's hands in space, on a massive field like Twickenham, and it's one-on-one or two-on-two, then that gets your attack going. So you can simplify it," Ford said.

"How many times can we get the ball in Will Joseph's hands this week? I want him to have double-figure touches. Same with Cadan, same with Max Ojomoh.

"When you are analysing, if you just bring it back to the simplest terms, these guys are unbelievable athletes with skill. So what do they need? They need time and space. So how do you get the ball to them in time and space? Just give it to them and let them go."

Live on BBC Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website and app

With Fin Smith rested, Ford is preferred to Marcus Smith at fly-half, with the latter again being deployed as a utility option off the bench.

For Ford, the debate around the England number 10s is nothing new.

"It's been like this all my England career. A lot has been spoken about fly-half in particular and who starts. And 12 years ago now when I first came in, it was the same," he said.

"Genuinely the three of us, our relationship, the respect we have for each other but how competitive we are as well, is probably the best I've experienced within the England team.

"We understand selection is very subjective and Steve will pick a 23 that he thinks is the best formula to win the game.

"For the team to succeed, for the team to win, for the team to go and win the Nations Championship or to go and win a World Cup in 12 months' time, it's going to need three high-quality, brilliant 10s who are great people as well.

"Fin has been amazing, the way he's played for Northampton, the way he's played for England, he's took it to a new level in his game.

"Marcus has started the season like a house on fire when he came back from his injury at Quins and you know what versatility he's got and how he can influence the game.

"And hopefully I can add when I am playing, when I'm not playing, maybe in a different kind of way.

"So what I'm saying is you get the one who's starting at the weekend, you probably get another one of us who's on the bench, but it's like a three-man job to get the team ready for every week. Of course we want to play, but we are very respectful of the situation."

articles.title: Scotland v Australia: Darcy Graham & Blair Kinghorn start for Gregor Townsend's side
articles.summary: Gregor Townsend stresses the importance of "individual responsibility" as Darcy Graham and Blair Kinghorn return to the Scotland XV against Australia.
articles.body:
Gregor Townsend has stressed the importance of "individual responsibility" before Sunday's Nations Championship fixture with Australia at Murrayfield (15:10 GMT).

The Scots conceded seven tries in defeat by New Zealand in Edinburgh last weekend, with the Wallabies losing to England at Twickenham.

Record try scorer Darcy Graham and Blair Kinghorn return to the Scotland XV, with Kinghorn taking over from Kyle Rowe at full-back and Jamie Dobie dropping to the bench to accommodate Graham on the wing. Rowe is not in the squad.

Graham, 29, was expected to miss the autumn Tests but has made a quicker-than-expected recovery from a bicep tear and returned to Edinburgh duty last month. He has 38 tries in 57 international appearances, while Toulouse's Kinghorn has 16 in 69 caps.

Townsend makes no changes to the starting pack while back-row Ollie Leatherbarrow could debut off the bench.

"The issues at the weekend were more about how we gave New Zealand opportunities within our 22, which had nothing to do really with what we did in defence," said Townsend.

"Well, someone coming offside or someone not rolling away quickly, yeah, it's part of the defence but that's more individual responsibility and making it harder for the opposition to get in our 22.

"And, yes, you have to make it as hard as possible when they're there but if you are giving those entries to the best teams in the world, they are looking to score over 50% of the time."

Australia head coach Les Kiss moves Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii from the wing to outside centre, with Harry Potter in at 11. Isaac Henry drops out, as does Declan Meredith, with Carter Gordon starting at fly-half.

In the pack, Jeremy Williams moves to lock in place of Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, with Rob Valetini coming in at blindside flanker.

articles.title: England respond to Eddie Jones mind games ahead of Japan match in Nations Championship
articles.summary: England scrum coach Tom Harrison denied his side will be distracted by their upcoming game against New Zealand ahead of facing Eddie Jones' Japan on Saturday at Twickenham; Cadan Murley looking to play his "best rugby" and hold down place in starting line-up
articles.body:
Jones is aiming to disrupt Steve Borthwick's side by hitting them with the unexpected in the belief they will be "a little bit distracted" by the All Blacks' visit to Allianz Stadium on November 21.

New Zealand are the box-office fixture of the campaign ahead of finals weekend but England deny they are looking beyond Japan.

"That's nowhere near the case because we understand how important this game is," scrum coach Tom Harrison said.

"We understand the challenge Japan can throw at us and we have to be alive in every single moment to the type of rugby they play.

"We understand that there might be unorthodox things coming our way but our need is to be alive.

"I've never worked with Eddie but I've met him a few times and he's a rugby genius, the way he thinks about the game and the way the players talk about him."

Murley: My best rugby will get me in the mix

Cadan Murley wins his eighth cap but first at Twickenham after coming in for the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso on the left wing as one of 10 changes made for Japan.

Murley, Max Ojomoh and Will Joseph are aiming to make an impression on Borthwick after the head coach signalled that places in next year's World Cup squad are up for grabs.

"I just want go out there and play my best rugby," Murley said. "I'll focus on what I can do, control the controllables, and hopefully that will get me in the mix further down the line.

"But my sole focus is on this game and putting my best foot forward. It's my first game at Twickenham and that's what's on my mind at the moment."

articles.title: Mako Vunipola: Leicester Tigers' ex-England prop exploring 'life after rugby' with coaching role
articles.summary: Former England prop Mako Vunipola talks about planning for his retirement by venturing into coaching at Leicester Tigers.
articles.body:
Former England prop Mako Vunipola says he started to plan for his retirement by venturing into coaching at Leicester Tigers.

The 35-year-old is juggling his playing duties at the East Midlands club with a coaching role with their Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) side.

Vunipola put his plans to hang up his boots on hold this season when he decided return to English rugby with Leicester after two years in France with Vannes.

The former Saracens front-rower also viewed the move as one that could help him prepare for what comes after his decorated playing career - including four Premiership titles and three European Champions Cup winners' medals - comes to an end.

"The rugby career is very short and it's time for me to start looking for what life looks like after rugby," he told BBC East Midlands Today.

"I wanted to explore the avenue of being a coach, so when Leicester spoke to me about coming to join the team I let them know that I'd like to transition into coaching.

"And they've been kind enough to help me in that process."

Vunipola planned to retire before Leicester called

Listen to the Tigers Rugby Show on BBC Radio Leicester

Vunipola's move to Leicester has him playing under former international team-mate Geoff Parling - a rugby boss who will be able to relate to what the prop is trying to do as an active player aspiring to be a coach.

Parling was emerging as a first-team player at Newcastle when he took on his first coaching job at university level, then later in his career, when playing for Exeter Chiefs, he worked with the Taunton Titans.

Vunipola has waited into the twilight of his playing career before turning some of his attention to coaching, which is an undertaking that has come with a few surprises.

"I thought rugby was just rugby and you just turn up and it's all the same, being a coach and a player. I had to quickly learn that it wasn't.

"It's been great to just be out there on the field in a different role trying learn how best I can become a coach."

And while he does that, he says his main focus remains on delivering for Tigers on the pitch.

Vunipola was a headline signing of the summer and has so far made six appearances across all competitions for a Tigers side top of the early Prem table.

"We're in the thick of the season and I'm just enjoying every moment as much as I can when I get the opportunity to play," he said.

The early months of Vunipola's time at Tigers have been dominated by what he can do as a player, but he has also got involved in Leicester's preparations for the upcoming PWR season as part of director of women's rugby Fraser Goatcher's support staff.

Goatcher says he is grateful for the "extra set of hands" - especially ones that have pulled on a British and Irish Lions shirt, while some players are a little more "starstruck" by Vunipola.

"I was a pretty big fan. He doesn't know that, but yeah it's been pretty special," said Tigers prop Ellie Smith.

"I grew up watching him, so having him as a coach has been a real privilege. And he has made a really big difference to my scrums.

"He has grown a lot as a coach. He was really quiet when he first came in, but now he talks all the time.

"He's really good at speaking with us girls and I think he's learned a lot about the girls programme that he didn't know before."

What Vunipola does know about rugby has come from some of the most astute minds in the world game.

And it is the knowledge accumulated from the who's who of head coaches and directors of rugby that he is keen to put to use - be it England boss Steve Borthwick, his predecessor Eddie Jones, ex-British and Irish Lions coach Warren Gatland or his successor Andy Farrell.

"They are all great coaches," Vunipola said.

"The coach I want to be is someone that can take bits from their coaching ability and add to it what I can. But that's a bit of a tough ask."

articles.title: England fly-half Harrison signs new Saracens deal
articles.summary: England fly-half Zoe Harrison renews her contract with Saracens for the forthcoming Premiership Women's Rugby campaign.
articles.body:
England fly-half Zoe Harrison has renewed her contract with Saracens for the forthcoming Premiership Women's Rugby campaign.

The 28-year-old has spent her entire professional career with the London side and started every game for England at last year's World Cup.

She went on to help Saracens win last season's PWR title as the league's leading points scorer, as well as being part of the England side that won the Six Nations in the spring.

"Zoe has established herself as one of the premier 10s in world rugby," Saracens director of rugby Alex Austerberry told the club website.

"Having represented the club well over 100 times and represented the Red Roses over 70 times she has great experience and this is invaluable when it comes to on-field and off-field management."

articles.title: Ireland v Fiji: Tadhg Beirne leads Irish bid to build on strong start to autumn campaign
articles.summary: Tadhg Beirne, so often Ireland's 'Mr Dependable', leads the team's bid to improve on last week's win over Argentina against Fiji on Saturday.
articles.body:
As Tadhg Beirne prepares to captain Ireland at home for the first time, it is worth recapping the impressive manner in which he has built up his CV in recent years.

Since missing the final three games of the Six Nations Grand Slam campaign in 2023 with an ankle injury, Beirne has missed just three Ireland Tests.

He was rested against Italy in 2024 and missed last year's summer meetings with Georgia and Portugal while on British and Irish Lions duty.

Such big-game ubiquity is not easily found in the modern game - and Beirne has often delivered in red and green.

He won the United Rugby Championship with Munster - his second league title after prevailing with Scarlets in 2017 - and was appointed the province's captain, replacing the legendary Peter O'Mahony.

A five-Test Lion, his performances in the back row for Farrell's tourists last year in Australia - playing every minute across the Test series win over the Wallabies - earned him the player of the series accolade.

A three-time member of World Rugby's men's 15s dream team of the year, Beirne was handed the Ireland captaincy for the first time in July's Nations Championship win over Japan, leading them to a 36-20 win.

Next year, adding to his fond memories down under as a key part of Ireland's World Cup squad will top his priority list.

Ulster's Timoney 'grateful' for Ireland chances

Nations Championship: Fixtures and standings

For now, though, the versatile forward is looking no further than the visit of Fiji to Dublin on Saturday as he bids to make it two wins from two as stand-in skipper.

"It's particularly special doing it at the Aviva, at home," said Beirne, who is deputising for the injured Caelan Doris and Dan Sheehan.

"I did have family over in Australia during the summer, but I'll have my family here, extended family and especially with this group, getting to lead those boys out is very cool and very special.

"My wife and daughter will be there, mum and dad will definitely be there, my sister – everyone who's in the country will be there, which is class.

"That's the nice part, leading up to the game, but I have a job to do and the folks will go through that, for sure. I'm really looking forward to it, it's a massive week for me and I am thoroughly enjoying it so far."

Live commentary on BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app

As he often does in green, Beirne played all 80 minutes of Ireland's commanding 42-12 win over Argentina in Dublin last week.

Against an underwhelming Pumas outfit, Ireland raced into a 21-5 half-time lead, and while they doubled their tally in the second half, in his post-match remarks Beirne admitted they "could have got a lot more out of" their autumn opener.

Now, with another week's training under the belt, Beirne says Ireland are determined to lay down another marker before next week's mouth-watering tussle with world champions South Africa.

"The big focus for us is to continue building on our performance, particularly from last week," he added.

"We laid down a foundation of how we want to play, but we're certainly not satisfied with that.

"Tomorrow is all about ourselves and making sure that we can play the way we want to play and put in a better performance over a longer period as well.

"I think there were patches of us playing really well there, but there were also patches where we weren't to the standard that we're going to hold ourselves to."

Beirne leads a side featuring seven personnel changes and two positional switches from the Argentina match, with Ronan Kelleher, James Ryan and Josh van der Flier recalled to the forward pack and Jamison Gibson-Park, Bundee Aki, Jamie Osborne and Tommy O'Brien drafted into the backline.

Nick Timoney and Mack Hansen switch to number eight and full-back respectively, with Beirne partnering Ryan in the second row.

Ireland, who sit third in the Nations Championship northern hemisphere table, have never lost to Fiji in a Test match and won 52-17 when the sides last met in Dublin in 2024.

The visitors - now coached by Jake White, who led South Africa to World Cup success in 2007 - have lost all four of their matches and were thrashed 54-17 by France in Lyon last week.
