articles.title: Wales v New Zealand: Chance to make a statement against All Blacks
articles.summary: Wales aim to make the rest of the world sit up and take notice when taking on resurgent New Zealand in the Nations Championship.
articles.body:
Andy Haden's dive, Joe Rokocoko's try double in a tight thriller, Alun Wyn Jones running out of steam after an interception, Andrew Hore getting away with a first-minute punch. What Wales would give for another sob story against New Zealand.

Steve Tandy's side have the latest shot at making history when they welcome the All Blacks to Principality Stadium in the Nations Championship (14:10 GMT).

That is the same price as Japan at England, while bookies prefer Fiji's chances in Ireland.

The likelihood is a 35th straight loss to New Zealand will be chalked up, with the streak of Welsh misery going into a 74th year since the victory in December 1953.

Tickets are still available for the fixture, which would have been unthinkable in past years when supporters feared missing history being made.

Is it defeatist to consider what would be a successful loss?

After spluttering to a 28-21 victory against Japan , and with morale low in the Welsh game courtesy of constant off-field turmoil , Wales must show something.

A year ago the score in the 48th minute was just 24-21 to New Zealand. Can Tandy's men make it to the hour with the unlikely still possible?

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and BBC Radio 5Live

Head coach Tandy has enjoyed victories against Japan twice, Fiji and Italy since taking the reins in 2025.

Wales' most recent victory of real significance was the 40-6 dismantling of Australia in the group stages of the 2023 World Cup under Warren Gatland.

The Wallabies are in town next Saturday (20:10 GMT) and that appears to present a better chance for a statement win, especially after their shocker against England last weekend.

Number eight Aaron Wainwright, who will be missed against New Zealand due to injury, stressed before the campaign that it is time to start making others sit up and take notice.

"It's about now we need to start putting in those performances that are going to make teams worried about us," he said before Wales failed to do that against Japan.

All Blacks aim to eliminate threat of Wales flanker Morgan

Cheating, scandal and drama - Wales agony v All Blacks

Wales were ranked eighth in the world when edged out 26-25 by New Zealand in 2004, a defeat that came a fortnight after a 38-36 loss to South Africa.

With 11 months to the start of the 2027 Rugby World Cup, time is running out to earn the respect of the teams that will travel to Australia with hopes of lifting the trophy.

"We want to push up the the rankings table, we want to get back into the top eight," said Wales captain Dewi Lake.

"You're looking at two teams [in New Zealand and Australia] that are sitting in there. It's an opportunity to see how we measure up."

The display against Japan did little to suggest that the gap to the elite is closing.

The mood in the Wales camp is upbeat and there is belief that progress is being made under Tandy and his new-look coaching team, albeit baby steps need to turn into strides.

"We were lucky last week that we were good enough to still win the game off the back of not performing as well as we wanted," admitted Lake.

"We've done a lot of work over the last year and a half on performance and we want to see that come to fruition.

"We know there are more levels in us and need to go there this weekend."

Tandy has tinkered with his team, with Wainwright's injury presenting a big opportunity for Taine Basham to take his Cardiff club form on to the international stage.

The 27-year-old from Talywain was Wales' star man against New Zealand in 2021 and this will be his first Test start since 2022.

The dynamic back-row forward must grasp his opportunity in the most fiercely competitive department of the squad.

Wales stick with the heavyweight centre partnership of Max Llewellyn and Eddie James, with the pressure on the set-piece to provide more of a platform.

The line-out struggled against Japan - who have top operators in Harry Hockings, Warner Dearns and Ben Gunter - but hooker Lake is confident it was just a bad day.

"Go back on our performances over the last 12 to 18 months and we've been one of the top teams in the world in that area," said the Gloucester captain.

"A lot of our tries have come from driving maul or line-out set plays. We have got backs who are dangerous on launch plays.

"When we do secure our set-piece we are a dangerous team. It was a setback last week but we'll put it right."

Montpellier lock Adam Beard, who is 6ft 8ins, returns to the side as line-out caller and Dragons co-captain Ben Carter drops to the bench.

Wales scored four tries in defeat by New Zealand last year when Tom Rogers made history with a hat-trick, with his fellow wing Louis Rees-Zammit getting the other with an acrobatic finish.

Rees-Zammit and full-back Blair Murray will aim to build on bright showings against Japan and have been joined by in-form Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb in the bid to give New Zealand a bloody nose.

"When you get the ball and get chances, be brave with it, be fearless because we have a strong back line and players who can finish," said Rees-Zammit.

Wales have only finished within a score of the All Blacks twice in 23 games since rugby union went professional in 1995.

In 2004 the defeat was by a point, with poor time management proving costly at the end, while in 2009 a chance to end the losing streak with a draw was lost when lock Jones was reeled in after an interception and then a last-gasp line-out went awry.

Better Wales teams than this one - Grand Slam winners and sides full of Lions - have failed to put the All Blacks under pressure.

New Zealand are hunting their fourth successive half-century in Cardiff after a 54-16 win in 2021, 55-23 in 2022 and 52-26 last year.

The second of those triumphs matched the All Blacks' highest points tally against Wales, a number they first hit in Hamilton in 2003.

It is a very one-sided rivalry but the magic of facing New Zealand, and facing the Haka, remains.

"I remember the 2013 year that they went unbeaten. They were a special team and will probably go down as the greatest ever," said lock Dafydd Jenkins about the double World Cup winning side.

"Everyone loved watching them. Brodie Retallick, Sam Whitelock, Kieran Read, Jerome Kaino and Richie McCaw – that back five will go down in history.

"When I was growing up, they were the South Africa of today and everyone hears stories about the famous black jersey.

"I've played with a few Kiwis at Exeter and they say how important it is to their culture. There's an aura around the All Blacks jersey."

The mood surrounding New Zealand is vastly different to 2025, when they travelled to Wales fresh from defeat by England.

The pressure and scrutiny on then boss Scott Robertson was intense as he twitchily carried out his pre-match media duties in their Cardiff bay hotel.

New Zealand eased to victory at Principality Stadium but it proved to be Robertson's last game in charge.

Dave Rennie was brought in as head coach and the former Glasgow boss appears to have made an immediate impact in game plan, clarity and culture.

New Zealand beat South Africa in Johannesburg and took plenty of positives despite being hit by a Springbok response in three defeats that followed.

After two wins against Australia and last week's second-half dominance against Scotland, the All Blacks will expect to ease past Wales before a mouthwatering game against England that is seen as the litmus test of their progress.

Beauden Barrett, who will captain New Zealand in a Test for the first time, warned against complacency.

"Wales are a team that want to play," said the full-back. "They've got plenty of excitement and some really big threats, especially out wide.

"They've certainly got a lot of grit, a lot of skill and X-factor, so we've got to be ready for anything."

New Zealand aim to overtake South Africa as leaders of the southern hemisphere table.

Wales players will back themselves to reward those who put their money on the 20-1 long shot, but most outside the camp would settle for making the visitors work for victory.

Replacements: Bell, Numia, Tosi, Hannah, E Blackadder, Fainga'anuku, Preston, R Ioane.

Assistants referees: Nic Berry (Australia) & Luc Ramos (France)

Who will Wales play at Twickenham finals weekend?

Wales have two fixtures remaining to decide their placing for finals day at Allianz Stadium.

It is possible that they could learn their Twickenham opponents this weekend with a round to play.

If Italy fail to beat Argentina with a bonus point on Saturday (11:40 GMT) then Wales will be guaranteed to finish at least fifth in the northern hemisphere table.

A Scotland bonus-point win against Australia on Sunday (15:10 GMT) would put fourth out of reach, and the Scots finish against Japan even if they slip up.

Wales are likely to finish fifth and play on Saturday, 28 November (13:10 GMT) in a double-header with the teams that finish second.

Another meeting with Japan looms unless Fiji win in Italy next weekend.

articles.title: Nations Championship - France 21-19 South Africa: Les Bleus put injuries behind them to hold on and stun Springboks in Paris
articles.summary: Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Théo Attissogbe, Louis Bielle-Biarrey score first-half tries for sensational France, who then withstand enormous second-half pressure from South Africa to secure Nations Championship victory and move closer to securing top spot in northern hemisphere table
articles.body:
The win is only the second for Les Bleus over the Springboks in the last 11 contests, with the hosts playing sensationally in the first half and digging in to survive and get over the line in the second.

Back-three Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Théo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey each scored tries in the opening half, with France belying the fact they had to play Antoine Dupont at 10 due to four fly-halves being out injured (Matthieu Jalibert, Romain Ntamack, Thomas Ramos, Antoine Hastoy).

All three tries were converted by Maxime Lucu, with France 21-7 ahead at the half-time break, but the second half proved entirely different.

Though South Africa were shown a 20-minute red card to back-row Cobus Wiese for an illegal ruck clear-out, France coughed up sin-bins to Lucu, Grandidier-Nkanang and Régis Montagne - the latter as a result of scrum penalties which kept flowing the visitors' way.

Scrum-half Cobus Reinach and hooker Malcom Marx scored tries in the second half for South Africa - adding to a first-half Jan-Hendrik Wessels effort - but Manie Libbok crucially missed the third conversion and the chance to draw level.

South Africa's wholesale front-row changes less than an hour before kick-off - swapping their starting front-row for their replacements - had ​little impact on France's fast start, with Dupont floating between fly-half and scrum-half from the off in a marvellous individual performance.

The match was considered a potential preview of the final at Twickenham in two weeks, but while France are closing in on representing the northern hemisphere - England and Ireland are now six points behind with two games to play - South Africa may not make it.

The Springboks will be overtaken atop the southern hemisphere standings and lose their No 1 world ranking if undefeated New Zealand beat Wales on Saturday in Cardiff, as expected.

On Friday, the Springboks closed to 21-14 with 30 minutes to go, revving up their power game for a grandstand finish.

France were bleeding penalties - nine in the scrum alone - but desperate scramble defence roused a packed Stade de France.

South Africa's Pieter-Steph du Toit was held up over the try-line late on, while Lucu - France's goalkicker with an 85 per cent success rate - ramped up the tension when he missed a straightforward penalty attempt that would have given France a 10-point lead.

Springboks hooker Marx inevitably scored from a rolling maul but Libbok, on for Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, botched the conversion attempt that would have levelled the score with eight minutes left.

The Boks had one last chance in the final minute, but Bielle-Biarrey stopped the charge and Dupont jumped on the loose ball, earning Lucu the chance to kick out and end a gripping Test match.

Dupont: We kept intensity up the whole match - 'That's huge for us'

France fly-half Antoine Dupont told ITV:

"I feel tired! They [South Africa] are really intense during the 80 minutes.

"It was so hard today with the yellow cards. We kept the intensity the whole game, and that's a huge thing for us today.

"We tried to adapt [Dupont at fly-half], we just had one day of training this week.

"I tried with Max [Lucu] to have the best combination possible. In attack and defence.

"With the energy of the entire team, it worked."

For France, they next face Argentina in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Stade de France in Paris on Saturday, November 21 (8.10pm kick-off).

South Africa travel to face Ireland at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin for their next Test, also on Saturday November 21 (4.40pm kick-off).

articles.title: France 21-19 South Africa: Les Bleus beat the world champions in Nations Championship
articles.summary: France hold on to end their five-match losing run against South Africa at Stade de France with an enthralling 21-19 victory in Paris.
articles.body:
Tries: Grandidier-Nkanang, Attissogbe, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Lucu (3)

Tries: Wessels, Reinach, Marx Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu (2)

France held on to end their five-match losing run against South Africa at Stade de France with an enthralling 21-19 victory in Paris.

The victory dents the world champions' hopes of reaching the Nations Championship final and puts Les Bleus in a strong position to top the northern hemisphere standings.

The hosts, inspired by their captain Antoine Dupont, showed their class and skill to score three first-half tries in an action-packed game.

France's back three of Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Theo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey all crossed in a thrilling opening 40 minutes, with Jan-Hendrik Wessels scoring off the back of a maul for the visitors.

The Springboks thought they had a second try on the stroke of half-time but Kurt-Lee Arendse's try was chalked off after he strayed marginally offside.

Number eight Jasper Wiese was shown a 20-minute red card early in the second half - the third of four cards shown the game - for a shoulder charge, but it had the opposite effect to derailing the world champions.

With South Africa's set-piece power proving too much, replacement scrum-half Cobus Reinach and hooker Malcolm Marx scored to set up a thrilling finale.

However, Manie Libbok missed the vital conversion to Marx's try that would have levelled the game.

With South Africa pushing for a winning score, Bielle-Biarrey produced a huge defensive tackle to force the ball loose, before Dupont, who was named player of the match, gathered possession to help seal the victory.

The result will come as a blow to both England and Ireland, who are in direct competition with France for a place in the Nations Championship final at the end of the month.

Les Bleus, who are six points clear at the top of the northern hemisphere standings, now face Argentina next Saturday, putting them in a strong position to reach the inaugural final at Allianz Stadium on Sunday, 29 November.

Injuries to France's three first-choice fly-halves - Matthieu Jalibert, Romain Ntamack and Antoine Hastoy - left France coach Fabien Galthie with little option but to deploy his captain and talismanic scrum-half at number 10.

Despite wearing the France number 10 shirt for the first time, Dupont lined up at scrum-half, as Galthie played Rassie Erasmus, who had swapped his entire front row an hour before kick-off, at his own game.

It was an electric start from the hosts, as a clever move sent Kalvin Gourgues through a gap, with Grandidier-Nkanang eventually crossing in the corner.

A monstrous left-footed 50:22 from Dupont, with South Africa lock Lood de Jager in the sin-bin for a high tackle, gave France field position, before the ball cannoned off Gourgues' head and Attissogbe crossed for a fortunate try.

Dupont supplied more magic, grubber kicking through on his stronger right foot for Bielle-Biarrey to race over.

South Africa's power told as they scored their opening try from a maul, before Erasmus changed his entire front row again, five minutes before half-time.

Creativity, intensity and physicality - it was a first game that felt remarkably similar to the epic quarter-final of the 2023 Rugby World Cup in Paris.

Despite losing Wiese to a 20-minute red card early in the second half, the world champions took advantage of Grandidier-Nkanang's sin-bin for a deliberate knock-on.

Tiredness and poor discipline made the game loose and chaotic, before the Springboks turned to their scrum to regain control.

A succession of scrum penalties resulted in another sin-bin, with replacement France prop Regis Montagne yellow carded as the hosts were left clinging on for the final 10 minutes.

Stunning scramble defence and sheer grit showed a side to the back-to-back Six Nations champions France that has often been questioned.

Despite their scrum crumbling, France held firm, continuing to chase kicks and compete for loose balls.

A draw would have felt a fair result given the contrasting nature of the two halves, but Libbok - as at the 2023 World Cup - badly shanked a kick that will once again raise questions over his ability to deliver under pressure in the biggest Test matches.

For once, the fine margins went against South Africa, who won every knockout game of the last World Cup by a point.

They face Ireland in Dublin next Saturday and will now likely need a favour from England, who take on New Zealand earlier that same day, if they are to reclaim top spot in the southern hemisphere standings.
